questions.question: Who was the President of India between the years 1987 and 1992?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**R Venkataraman**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **R Venkataraman** served as the 8th President of India from **25 July 1987 to 25 July 1992**.
 
• He was elected as President by the **Electoral College of India**, consisting of elected members of both houses of Parliament and Legislative Assemblies of States and Union territories.
 
• Prior to his presidency, Venkataraman held significant positions, including **Vice President of India** and **Minister of Defence**.
 
• He was awarded the **Padma Vibhushan** in 1988 for his services to the nation.
 
• Venkataraman played a crucial role in India’s political landscape during his tenure, emphasizing stability and constitutional values.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Electoral College**

 
 
• The President of India is elected by an electoral college consisting of elected members of both houses of Parliament and Legislative Assemblies of States and Union territories.
 
• The election follows the system of proportional representation by means of a single transferable vote.
 
• The process ensures uniformity in representation of different states.
 
 
 
• **Vice President of India**
 
 
• The Vice President is the second-highest constitutional office in India, succeeding the President.
 
• The Vice President also serves as the ex-officio Chairman of the Rajya Sabha (Council of States).
 
• The term of the Vice President is five years, and they can be re-elected.
 
 
 
• **Padma Vibhushan**
 
 
• The Padma Vibhushan is the second-highest civilian award in India.
 
• It is awarded for exceptional and distinguished service in any field including government service.
 
• The awards are announced every year on Republic Day (26th January).
 
 
 
• **Constitutional Values**
 
 
• Constitutional values refer to the fundamental principles and ideals upon which the Indian Constitution is based.
 
• These include justice, liberty, equality, and fraternity.
 
• Presidents of India play a crucial role in upholding these values through their office and actions.

questions.question: Buddhist texts called Dipavamsa and Mahavamsa, which are the sources of information to Mauryan times, belong to which of the following countries?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Sri Lanka**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The **Dipavamsa** and **Mahavamsa** are ancient Buddhist texts written in Pali.
 
• These texts are considered the earliest historical records of Sri Lanka.
 
• The Mahavamsa was composed in the 5th century AD, while the Dipavamsa predates it, being compiled in the 4th century AD.
 
• Both texts provide detailed accounts of the history of Buddhism in Sri Lanka, as well as the island's political and cultural history.
 
• These chronicles are essential sources of historical information about the reign of the Mauryan Emperor Ashoka and his role in the spread of Buddhism.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Dipavamsa**

 
 
• The Dipavamsa, meaning "Chronicle of the Island," is the earliest extant chronicle of Sri Lanka.
 
• It provides accounts of the early history of Buddhism in Sri Lanka, including the arrival of Buddhism on the island.
 
• The text is believed to have been compiled by Buddhist monks of the Mahavihara tradition.
 
• It serves as a precursor to the more comprehensive Mahavamsa.
 
 
 
• **Mahavamsa**
 
 
• The Mahavamsa, meaning "Great Chronicle," was composed by the Buddhist monk Mahanama in the 5th century AD.
 
• This chronicle covers the history of Sri Lanka from the legendary past up to the reign of King Mahasena (334-361 AD).
 
• The Mahavamsa is divided into three parts: the Mahavamsa, the Culavamsa, and the modern continuation of the chronicle.
 
• It is considered a vital source for understanding the historical and cultural development of Sri Lanka.
 
 
 
• **Role of Emperor Ashoka**
 
 
• Emperor Ashoka of the Maurya Dynasty played a crucial role in the spread of Buddhism to Sri Lanka.
 
• He sent his son Mahinda and daughter Sanghamitta to Sri Lanka to spread Buddhist teachings.
 
• The Mahavamsa provides detailed accounts of their missions and the establishment of Buddhism on the island.
 
 
 
• **Pali Language**
 
 
• Pali is the liturgical language of Theravada Buddhism and was used to compose the early Buddhist scriptures.
 
• The Dipavamsa and Mahavamsa are significant historical texts written in Pali.
 
• Pali is closely related to Sanskrit and was widely used in ancient India and Sri Lanka.

questions.question:
Read the given statements and select the correct option regarding ‘High Powered Money’.

(i) High Powered Money consists of currency and cash reserves with the bank.

(ii) High Powered Money includes demand deposits of the banks.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Only (i) is true**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• High Powered Money, also known as the monetary base, consists of currency in circulation and cash reserves held by the banks.
 
• It includes the total currency issued by the central bank and held by the public plus the deposits held by commercial banks with the central bank.
 
• Demand deposits are not included in High Powered Money; they are part of the broader money supply categories such as M1, M2, etc.
 
• High Powered Money is crucial because it serves as the foundation upon which the money supply is built through the banking system.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Monetary Base (High Powered Money)**

 
 
• It is the sum of currency in circulation and reserves held by banks with the central bank.
 
• It is a critical measure used by central banks to control the money supply and manage economic stability.
 
 
 
• **Money Supply**
 
 
• The total amount of monetary assets available in an economy at a specific time.
 
• Common measures of money supply include M1 (currency and demand deposits), M2 (M1 plus savings deposits), etc.
 
 
 
• **Central Bank Reserves**
 
 
• Deposits that commercial banks hold with the central bank as part of their required reserves.
 
• These reserves are used to meet the liquidity needs and regulatory requirements.
 
 
 
• **Currency in Circulation**
 
 
• The physical money (coins and paper currency) held by the public and businesses, excluding the reserves held by banks.
 
• It forms part of the broader money supply and is directly controlled by the central bank.

• The task force included experts from various fields to ensure a comprehensive approach to policy formulation.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **NABARD**

 
 
• Established on **12 July 1982** by a special Act of the Parliament.
 
• It is an apex development financial institution in India, headquartered in Mumbai.
 
• The primary objective is to **provide and regulate credit** for the promotion of agriculture, small-scale industries, cottage and village industries, and other rural crafts.
 
• It also plays a key role in implementing various government schemes and initiatives aimed at rural development.
 
 
 
• **Microfinance**
 
 
• Microfinance refers to financial services, such as **microloans, savings, insurance, and fund transfers**, offered to low-income individuals or groups.
 
• It aims to **provide access to financial resources** for those who do not have access to traditional banking services.
 
• Microfinance institutions (MFIs) play a crucial role in the economic development of underserved communities.
 
• It has been recognized as an effective tool for **poverty alleviation and economic empowerment**.
 
 
 
• **Microfinance Institutions (MFIs)**
 
 
• MFIs are financial institutions that provide **microfinance services** to the underserved population.
 
• They include a variety of entities such as non-governmental organizations (NGOs), cooperatives, and commercial banks.
 
• The primary focus is on providing small loans (microloans) to individuals or groups, usually to start or expand small businesses.
 
• MFIs also offer other financial services such as **savings accounts, insurance, and money transfer services**.
 
 
 
• **Role of NABARD in Microfinance**
 
 
• NABARD provides **financial support and capacity-building** for MFIs.
 
• It facilitates the formation and nurturing of Self-Help Groups (SHGs).
 
• NABARD also provides **refinance support** to banks for lending to the microfinance sector.
 
• It has been instrumental in the development and implementation of various microfinance models in India.

questions.question: Which component of the cytoskeleton are rigid hollow rods, about 25 nm in diameter, that play an important role in the cell cycle by forming the mitotic spindle?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Microtubules**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Microtubules** are rigid hollow rods that are approximately 25 nm in diameter.
 
• They play a crucial role in the cell cycle by forming the **mitotic spindle**.
 
• Microtubules are composed of tubulin proteins, specifically alpha and beta tubulin.
 
• They help in maintaining cell shape, enabling intracellular transport, and separating chromosomes during cell division.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Intermediate filaments**

 
 
• Intermediate filaments are about 10 nm in diameter and provide mechanical support for the cell.
 
• They are composed of various proteins such as keratins, vimentin, and lamins.
 
 
 
• **Actin filaments**
 
 
• Actin filaments, also known as microfilaments, are about 7 nm in diameter and are composed of actin protein.
 
• They are involved in cell movement and shape changes, as well as muscle contraction.
 
 
 
• **Cell cycle**
 
 
• The cell cycle consists of interphase (G1, S, G2 phases) and mitotic phase (M phase).
 
• Microtubules are critical during the M phase for the separation of chromosomes.
 
 
 
• **Tubulin**
 
 
• Tubulin is the protein building block of microtubules.
 
• Alpha and beta tubulin dimers polymerize to form the microtubule structure.

questions.question: Under which Act was the legislative powers of making and amending laws restored to the provinces?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Indian Council Act, 1861**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The Indian Council Act of 1861 was a significant step towards the decentralization of legislative powers in British India.
 
• It restored legislative powers to the provinces, allowing them to make and amend laws for their respective regions.
 
• This Act introduced legislative councils at the provincial level, which included nominated Indian members, thereby giving Indians a limited role in governance.
 
• The Act was instrumental in laying the foundation for the creation of future legislative structures in India, leading to more autonomous provincial governance.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Indian Council Act, 1892**

 
 
• This Act increased the number of non-official members in the Central and Provincial Legislative Councils.
 
• It allowed for discussion of the budget and addressing questions to the executive.
 
• However, it did not grant any legislative powers to the members.
 
 
 
• **Indian Council Act, 1909**
 
 
• Also known as the Morley-Minto Reforms, this Act introduced separate electorates for Muslims.
 
• It increased the size of legislative councils and expanded the role of Indians in the governance process.
 
 
 
• **Regulating Act, 1773**
 
 
• This was the first attempt by the British Parliament to regulate the East India Company's rule in India.
 
• It established a system of dual governance in Bengal and created the position of Governor-General of Bengal.

questions.question: Guru Vempati Chinna Satyam is associated with which of these dance forms?

• It combines fast rhythms with fluid movements, creating a unique blend of control and abandon.
 
• The dance often includes storytelling through expressive gestures and intricate footwork.
 
• Traditionally, Kuchipudi was performed by male dancers in temples as a form of worship.
 
• It incorporates elements of drama and has a strong narrative aspect, often depicting mythological tales.

• His choreographies include classical pieces such as "Bhama Kalapam" and "Rukmini Kalyanam."
 
• He trained numerous disciples who have carried forward his legacy globally.

questions.question: ____ refers to the measure related to the sale of assets for the achievement of some purpose.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Liquidation**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Liquidation is the process of bringing a business to an end and distributing its assets to claimants.
 
• It typically occurs when a company is insolvent, meaning it cannot pay its obligations as and when they come due.
 
• The assets of the company are sold off and the proceeds are used to pay off debts, liabilities, and expenses.
 
• Any remaining funds are distributed to the shareholders of the company.
 
• Liquidation can be voluntary or involuntary, depending on whether the decision is made by the shareholders or forced by creditors through court action.

• **Voluntary Liquidation**
 
 
• Voluntary liquidation occurs when the shareholders of a company decide to wind up its affairs and dissolve the company.
 
• This decision is often made when a company has fulfilled its purpose or when it is financially beneficial to dissolve the entity.
 
• The process involves selling off the company's assets, paying off creditors, and distributing any remaining funds to shareholders.
 
 
 
• **Involuntary Liquidation**
 
 
• Involuntary liquidation occurs when creditors force a company into liquidation through court action due to unpaid debts.
 
• This type of liquidation is often initiated when creditors believe they will not recover their funds through normal business operations.
 
• The court appoints a liquidator to sell off the company's assets and distribute the proceeds to creditors.

questions.question: Which of the following Articles of the Indian Constitution, related to fundamental rights, CANNOT be suspended during an emergency?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Articles 20-21**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Articles 20 and 21 of the Indian Constitution deal with the protection of certain rights regarding conviction for offenses and the protection of life and personal liberty.
 
• Article 20 provides protection against arbitrary and excessive punishment to an accused person, ensuring the right against ex post facto laws, double jeopardy, and self-incrimination.
 
• Article 21 guarantees the right to life and personal liberty, stating that no person shall be deprived of his life or personal liberty except according to the procedure established by law.
 
• During an emergency, these fundamental rights (Articles 20-21) cannot be suspended as per the provisions of the Constitution.
 
• The Supreme Court of India has reiterated the inviolability of these rights even during periods of emergency, maintaining their protection.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Emergency Provisions in India:**

 
 
• The Indian Constitution provides for three types of emergencies: National Emergency (Article 352), State Emergency (Article 356), and Financial Emergency (Article 360).
 
• During a national emergency, fundamental rights under Article 19 are suspended, but Articles 20 and 21 remain protected.
 
• State emergency, also known as President's Rule, can be imposed when a state government is unable to function according to the Constitution.
 
• Financial emergency can be declared if the financial stability or credit of India is threatened.
 
 
 
• **Article 19:**
 
 
• Article 19 guarantees six fundamental freedoms: speech and expression, assembly, association, movement, residence, and profession.
 
• These rights can be suspended during a national emergency.
 
• Article 19 is a critical component of the fundamental rights provided under Part III of the Constitution.
 
 
 
• **Supreme Court Judgments:**
 
 
• The Supreme Court has played a pivotal role in safeguarding fundamental rights during emergencies.
 
• Key judgments include the landmark case of Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India, which expanded the interpretation of Article 21.
 
• In ADM Jabalpur v. Shivkant Shukla, the Court initially upheld suspension of habeas corpus during emergency, but this was later criticized and overturned in subsequent judgments.
 
 
 
• **Constitutional Amendments:**
 
 
• The 44th Amendment Act, 1978, was significant in ensuring that Articles 20 and 21 cannot be suspended even during emergencies.
 
• This amendment provided greater protection to the fundamental rights of individuals.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Fundamental Duties:**

 
 
• The Fundamental Duties were added to the Indian Constitution by the 42nd Amendment Act, 1976, upon the recommendations of the Swaran Singh Committee.
 
• Originally, 10 duties were listed, and an 11th duty was added by the 86th Amendment Act, 2002.
 
 
 
• **42nd Amendment Act, 1976:**
 
 
• Known as the "Mini-Constitution" due to its wide-ranging amendments.
 
• It added the Fundamental Duties and also introduced changes to the Preamble, among other significant changes.
 
 
 
• **Scientific Temper:**
 
 
• Scientific temper refers to an attitude of logical and rational thinking.
 
• It involves questioning, observing physical reality, testing, hypothesizing, analyzing, and communicating.
 
 
 
• **Non-Justiciable Nature:**
 
 
• Fundamental Duties are not enforceable by law, unlike Fundamental Rights.
 
• They serve as moral obligations for the citizens to promote a spirit of patriotism and uphold the unity of India.

• Swami Vivekananda founded the **Ramakrishna Mission** on 1 May 1897.
 
• The organization was established to carry forward the teachings of **Sri Ramakrishna Paramhansa**, his spiritual teacher.
 
• The mission's headquarters are located at **Belur Math**, on the western bank of the Hooghly River, near Kolkata, India.
 
• The Ramakrishna Mission focuses on religious, educational, and philanthropic activities, emphasizing the philosophy of **Vedanta**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

• He was a 19th-century Indian mystic and saint whose teachings inspired the formation of the Ramakrishna Mission.
 
• He emphasized the unity of all religions and the importance of personal spiritual experience.
 
• His teachings were propagated by his disciple, Swami Vivekananda, who played a crucial role in spreading Vedanta philosophy in the West.
 
 
 
• **Vedanta Philosophy**
 
 
• Vedanta is one of the six orthodox schools of Hindu philosophy.

• Belur Math is the headquarters of the Ramakrishna Math and Mission.
 
• It was established by Swami Vivekananda in 1898.
 
• Belur Math is a pilgrimage site and an architectural marvel that symbolizes the unity of all religions.
 
 
 
• **Interfaith Understanding**
 
 
• Swami Vivekananda promoted the idea that all religions are different paths to the same divine goal.
 
• His famous speech at the Parliament of the World's Religions in Chicago in 1893 emphasized religious tolerance and universal acceptance.

questions.question: ______ wrote a three-volume history of Akbar’s reign, titled ‘Akbar Nama’.

__
 
• **Abul Fazl** was a prominent historian and courtier in the court of Mughal Emperor Akbar.
 
• He authored the **three-volume history of Akbar's reign**, known as the **Akbar Nama**.
 
• The **Akbar Nama** is a detailed chronicle of Akbar's life and the history of his reign, written in Persian.
 
• Abul Fazl was also one of the nine jewels (Navaratnas) in Akbar's court.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Akbar Nama**

 
 
• The work is divided into three volumes: the first volume deals with Akbar's ancestors, the second volume records the events of Akbar's reign, and the third volume is the Ain-i-Akbari, which provides detailed information about the administration of the empire.
 
• The **Ain-i-Akbari** is a valuable resource for understanding the administrative system, culture, and society of the Mughal Empire.
 
• The Akbar Nama is considered one of the most important sources of Mughal history.
 
 
 
• **Abul Fazl's Contributions**
 
 
• Besides the Akbar Nama, Abul Fazl also played a crucial role in the administration and cultural development of Akbar's empire.

• Abul Fazl's writings reflect his deep knowledge of Persian literature, history, and governance.

questions.question: Under which of the following Articles can a person directly approach the Supreme Court for the enforcement of his Fundamental Rights?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Article 32**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Article 32** of the Indian Constitution provides the right to individuals to move the Supreme Court directly for the enforcement of their fundamental rights.
 
• Dr. B.R. Ambedkar referred to Article 32 as the "heart and soul" of the Constitution, emphasizing its importance in upholding fundamental rights.
 
• Article 32 guarantees the right to constitutional remedies, empowering the Supreme Court to issue writs such as habeas corpus, mandamus, prohibition, quo warranto, and certiorari for the enforcement of these rights.
 
• This provision ensures that the fundamental rights are not merely theoretical but can be practically enforced through the highest court in India.
 
• Any individual whose fundamental rights are violated can directly approach the Supreme Court without having to go through lower courts first.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Fundamental Rights**

 
 
• These are a set of rights granted to all citizens by the Indian Constitution, aimed at ensuring individual liberty and equality.
 
• There are six fundamental rights: Right to Equality, Right to Freedom, Right against Exploitation, Right to Freedom of Religion, Cultural and Educational Rights, and Right to Constitutional Remedies.
 
 
 
• **Writs**
 
 
• Habeas Corpus: A writ requiring a person to be brought before a judge or court, especially to secure the person's release unless lawful grounds are shown for their detention.
 
• Mandamus: A writ issued as a command to an inferior court or ordering a person to perform a public or statutory duty.
 
• Prohibition: A writ directing a subordinate to stop doing something the law prohibits.
 
• Quo Warranto: A writ requiring a person to show by what warrant an office or franchise is held, claimed, or exercised.
 
• Certiorari: A writ by which a higher court reviews a case tried in a lower court.
 
 
 
• **Judicial Review**
 
 
• The power of the judiciary to review and determine the validity of a law or an order.
 
• It helps in upholding the supremacy of the Constitution and ensuring the protection of fundamental rights.
 
 
 
• **Supreme Court of India**
 
 
• The apex judicial body in India, established in 1950.
 
• It has the power to interpret the Constitution and enforce the fundamental rights of citizens.
 
• The decisions of the Supreme Court are binding on all courts within India.

questions.question: Mount Fuji, the highest mountain in Japan, which is made of felsic to intermediate rock, represents which type of volcanoes?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Composite**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Mount Fuji is classified as a composite volcano, also known as a stratovolcano.
 
• Composite volcanoes are characterized by a conical shape formed from multiple layers of hardened lava, tephra, pumice, and volcanic ash.
 
• They typically feature steep profiles and periodic, explosive eruptions.
 
• Examples of other well-known composite volcanoes include Mount St. Helens in the USA and Mount Vesuvius in Italy.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Volcano Types**

 
 
• **Shield Volcano:** These volcanoes have gentle slopes and are primarily built up by the flow of low-viscosity basaltic lava.
 
• **Cinder Cone:** These are the smallest type of volcanoes, built from particles and blobs of congealed lava ejected from a single vent.
 
• **Fissure Volcano:** These volcanoes erupt from long cracks in the ground rather than a central vent, producing large quantities of basaltic lava.
 
 
 
• **Volcanic Eruption Styles:**
 
 
• **Effusive Eruptions:** Characterized by the outpouring of lava onto the ground.
 
• **Explosive Eruptions:** Involve the violent release of gases and pyroclastic material.
 
 
 
• **Mount Fuji Facts**
 
 
• Mount Fuji last erupted in 1707-1708, during the Edo period.
 
• It is a cultural icon of Japan and is frequently depicted in art and photography.
 
 
 
• **Volcanic Hazards:**
 
 
• Volcanic eruptions can produce lava flows, ash fall, pyroclastic flows, and volcanic bombs.
 
• Secondary effects include lahars (volcanic mudflows) and tsunamis.

questions.question: Identify the Navratna of Akbar’s court who played a pivotal role in the development of the classical genre of Hindustani music.

• **Tansen**, also known as Miyan Tansen, was one of the nine gems (Navratnas) in the court of Emperor Akbar.
 
• He is widely considered as a pioneer in the development of the classical genre of Hindustani music.
 
• Tansen was known for his ability to create ragas and for his mesmerizing performances.
 
• He is often credited with composing several new ragas and perfecting the dhrupad style of singing.
 
• His contributions significantly shaped the future of Indian classical music, making him a legendary figure in the field.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

• The Navratnas were nine extraordinary talents in Akbar's court, each excelling in different fields such as literature, music, and administration.

• **Hindustani Classical Music:**
 
 
• It is one of the two major traditions of Indian classical music, the other being Carnatic music from the South.
 
• Hindustani music places a strong emphasis on improvisation and exploring all aspects of a raga.
 
 
 
• **Ragas:**

questions.question: In 1991, India met with an economic crisis due to ________.

options.text: the rise in foreign exchange reserves

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**huge debts burden**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• In 1991, India faced a severe economic crisis primarily due to a **huge debt burden** accumulated over the years.
 
• The country had **high fiscal deficits** and was unable to meet its external debt obligations.
 
• India's **foreign exchange reserves** were rapidly depleting, falling to levels that could barely cover three weeks' worth of imports.
 
• To avert the crisis, India had to secure an emergency loan from the **International Monetary Fund (IMF)** by pledging its gold reserves.
 
• This economic turmoil led to significant economic reforms and liberalization policies to open up the Indian economy.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Fiscal Deficit**

 
 
• Fiscal deficit occurs when a government's total expenditures exceed the revenue that it generates, excluding money from borrowings.
 
• It is an important indicator of a government's financial health and economic stability.
 
 
 
• **Balance of Payments (BoP) Crisis**
 
 
• The Balance of Payments crisis refers to a situation where a country cannot pay for essential imports or service its debt repayments.
 
• It often leads to a sharp decline in the value of the country's currency.
 
 
 
• **International Monetary Fund (IMF)**
 
 
• The IMF is an international financial institution headquartered in Washington, D.C.
 
• It aims to foster global monetary cooperation, secure financial stability, facilitate international trade, promote high employment, and reduce poverty.
 
 
 
• **Economic Liberalization in India**
 
 
• The 1991 economic reforms marked a significant shift in India's economic policy, moving from a closed economy to an open-market economy.
 
• Key reforms included deregulation, reducing import tariffs, and opening up to foreign investments.
 
• The liberalization policies helped in accelerating economic growth and improving the overall economic health of the country.

questions.question: Which of the following layers is important for living things?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Troposphere**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The troposphere is the lowest layer of Earth's atmosphere and extends up to about 8-15 kilometers above sea level.
 
• It contains approximately 75% of the atmosphere's mass and 99% of its water vapor and aerosols.
 
• This layer is crucial for weather phenomena, including clouds, rain, and storms, which directly affect life on Earth.
 
• The troposphere supports life by providing the necessary gases like oxygen for respiration and carbon dioxide for photosynthesis.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Stratosphere:**

 
 
• The stratosphere is the second layer of Earth's atmosphere, situated above the troposphere and below the mesosphere.
 
• It contains the ozone layer, which absorbs and scatters ultraviolet solar radiation, protecting living organisms from harmful UV rays.
 
 
 
• **Mesosphere:**
 
 
• The mesosphere is the third layer of the atmosphere, located above the stratosphere and below the thermosphere.
 
• Meteors burn up in this layer due to the increased density of atmospheric gases.
 
 
 
• **Thermosphere:**
 
 
• The thermosphere is the fourth layer and lies above the mesosphere, extending up to the exosphere.
 
• This layer is characterized by high temperatures caused by the absorption of highly energetic solar radiation.
 
 
 
• **Exosphere:**
 
 
• The exosphere is the outermost layer of Earth's atmosphere, where atmospheric particles are so sparse that they can travel hundreds of kilometers without colliding.
 
• It gradually fades into outer space and is primarily composed of hydrogen and helium.

questions.question: During the Fourth Five-Year Plan, the process of nationalisation of banks took place. How many banks were nationalised during this period?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**14**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The process of nationalisation of banks during the Fourth Five-Year Plan (1969-1974) was a significant move in India's banking history.
 
• A total of 14 major commercial banks were nationalised by the Indian government on 19 July 1969.
 
• This move aimed to align banking operations with the economic and social goals of the country, ensuring better control over credit delivery.
 
• The nationalisation targeted banks with deposits of Rs. 50 crores or more, bringing them under the control of the government.
 
• It marked a pivotal step towards the expansion and spread of banking facilities across the rural and semi-urban areas of India.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Nationalisation of Banks:**

 
 
• Refers to the process where private sector banks are transferred into public ownership by the government.
 
• The primary objective was to ensure sufficient credit for agriculture, small industry, and exports, and to promote banking habits among the population.
 
 
 
• **Fourth Five-Year Plan (1969-1974):**
 
 
• Focused on growth with stability and progressive achievement of self-reliance.
 
• It aimed at accelerating the process of industrialisation and growth of the agricultural sector.
 
 
 
• **Impact of Nationalisation:**
 
 
• Led to significant branch expansion and increased access to banking services in rural and semi-urban areas.
 
• Facilitated better implementation of government policies and schemes aimed at poverty alleviation and rural development.
 
 
 
• **Subsequent Nationalisation:**
 
 
• A second wave of nationalisation occurred in April 1980, when six more commercial banks were nationalised.
 
• This brought the total number of nationalised banks in India to 20.

questions.question: What is the tenure of the President of India?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**5 years**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The President of India is elected for a term of **5 years** according to Article 56 of the Indian Constitution.
 
• The election process for the President is outlined in Article 54 and Article 55 of the Indian Constitution.
 
• The term of the President can be extended if the elections are not completed before the expiry of the term, as per Article 56(1)(c).
 
• A President can be re-elected and there is no limit on the number of terms a person can serve as President.
 
• The President continues to hold office until his successor is duly elected and enters office.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Election Procedure:**

 
 
• The President is elected by an Electoral College consisting of elected members of both houses of Parliament as well as the elected members of the Legislative Assemblies of States and Union territories.
 
• The voting is done by secret ballot using the single transferable vote system.
 
 
 
• **Eligibility Criteria:**
 
 
• A candidate must be a citizen of India, at least 35 years old, and qualified to be a member of the Lok Sabha.
 
• He/she should not hold any office of profit under the Government of India, a state government, or any public authority.
 
 
 
• **Impeachment:**
 
 
• The President can be removed from office through a process called impeachment for violation of the Constitution.
 
• The impeachment process can be initiated in either House of Parliament and requires a two-thirds majority in both houses.
 
 
 
• **Oath of Office:**
 
 
• The President takes an oath or affirmation before entering upon the office, which is administered by the Chief Justice of India or the senior-most judge of the Supreme Court available.

questions.question: In which of the following years was the Vernacular Press Act passed?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**1878**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The Vernacular Press Act was enacted in **1878** by Lord Lytton, the then Viceroy of India.
 
• The Act was aimed at curbing the freedom of the Indian-language press and was considered a repressive measure.
 
• It empowered the government to confiscate the printing presses, paper, and other materials of the native press if it published anything that was deemed seditious.
 
• The Act was specifically targeted at the Indian press and excluded the English-language publications.
 
• The Vernacular Press Act was repealed in **1882** by Lord Ripon, who succeeded Lord Lytton as Viceroy of India.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Background of the Act:**

 
 
• The growing influence of the Indian press during the 1870s led the British government to introduce the Vernacular Press Act to control anti-British sentiments.
 
• Indian newspapers had started to criticize British policies, which alarmed the colonial administration.
 
 
 
• **Impact on Indian Journalism:**
 
 
• The Act imposed severe restrictions on the Indian press, leading to widespread protests and resentment among Indian journalists and nationalists.
 
• It marked a significant moment in the history of the Indian freedom struggle, emphasizing the need for freedom of expression.
 
 
 
• **Repeal of the Act:**
 
 
• Lord Ripon, known for his liberal policies, repealed the Vernacular Press Act in 1882, restoring press freedom to some extent.
 
• This repeal was welcomed by Indian leaders and helped to reduce some of the tensions between the British government and the Indian populace.
 
 
 
• **Legacy:**
 
 
• The Vernacular Press Act is often cited as an example of colonial repression, and its history is studied in the context of the freedom of the press in India.
 
• It remains a significant event that highlighted the power of the press and its role in shaping public opinion.

questions.question: Which of the following powers is NOT enjoyed by the Governor of a State?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Diplomatic/Military powers**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The Governor of a state in India does not have any Diplomatic or Military powers.
 
• These powers are exclusively reserved for the President of India.
 
• The Governor's role is limited to the state level and does not extend to international or military affairs.
 
• Diplomatic powers include appointing ambassadors, entering into treaties, and conducting foreign relations, all of which are managed by the central government.
 
• Military powers include the command of the armed forces, which is vested in the President as the supreme commander.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Judiciary Powers of Governor:**

 
 
• The Governor has the power to grant pardons, reprieves, respites, or remission of punishment.
 
• He can also suspend, remit or commute the sentence of any person convicted of any offense against state laws.
 
 
 
• **Executive Powers of Governor:**
 
 
• The Governor appoints the Chief Minister and other ministers.
 
• He appoints the Advocate General and the State Election Commissioner.
 
• All executive actions of the state are taken in the name of the Governor.
 
 
 
• **Legislative Powers of Governor:**
 
 
• The Governor can summon, prorogue, and dissolve the state legislative assembly.
 
• He addresses the state legislature at the commencement of the first session after each general election.
 
• The Governor can reserve certain bills for the President's consideration.
 
 
 
• **Financial Powers of Governor:**
 
 
• The Governor ensures that the Annual Financial Statement (State Budget) is laid before the state legislature.
 
• No money bill can be introduced in the state legislature without the Governor's prior recommendation.

questions.question: For which of the following dance forms was Gaddam Padmaja Reddy awarded the Padma Shri in 2022?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Kuchipudi**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Gaddam Padmaja Reddy is a renowned exponent of the Kuchipudi dance form, a classical Indian dance originating from Andhra Pradesh.
 
• She was awarded the Padma Shri in 2022 for her significant contributions to the Kuchipudi dance.
 
• Padmaja Reddy has been instrumental in popularizing Kuchipudi both in India and internationally through her performances and teachings.
 
• The Padma Shri is one of the highest civilian awards in India, recognizing distinguished contributions in various fields, including the arts.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Kuchipudi Dance**

 
 
• Kuchipudi is a classical dance form from Andhra Pradesh, known for its intricate footwork and expressive gestures.
 
• It combines dance, music, and acting, often depicting stories from Hindu epics such as the Ramayana and Mahabharata.
 
• This dance form was traditionally performed by male Brahmins in temples, but it is now practiced by both men and women.
 
• Key elements of Kuchipudi include rhythmic patterns (jatis), expressive dance (nritya), and dramatic storytelling (natya).
 
 
 
• **Padma Awards**
 
 
• The Padma Awards, comprising Padma Vibhushan, Padma Bhushan, and Padma Shri, are among the highest civilian honors in India.
 
• These awards are announced annually on the occasion of Republic Day and recognize achievements in various fields such as arts, literature, sports, medicine, social work, science, and public affairs.
 
• The Padma Shri is the fourth highest civilian award in India, honoring exceptional service in any field.
 
 
 
• **Indian Classical Dance Forms**
 
 
• India is home to several classical dance forms, each with its unique style, music, and cultural significance.
 
• Some of the prominent classical dance forms include Bharatanatyam, Kathak, Odissi, Manipuri, Mohiniyattam, Kathakali, and Sattriya.
 
• These dance forms often incorporate elements of storytelling, devotional themes, and intricate choreography.
 
 
 
• **Importance of Classical Dance**
 
 
• Classical dance forms are a vital part of India's cultural heritage, preserving traditional art and storytelling.
 
• They play a significant role in promoting cultural awareness and appreciation both nationally and internationally.
 
• Classical dance training often involves rigorous practice and dedication, emphasizing discipline and artistic expression.
